EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A prolonged period of deep moist southwesterly flow from the North Pacific ocean, otherwise known as an Atmospheric River, produced several days of heavy rainfall along the south slopes of the Brooks Range. event_description: Press Release -2025 Late August Storm Disaster Declaration and Recovery Assistance (9/5/2025)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An atmospheric river moved up from the North Pacific into Southcentral Alaska and produced widespread moderate rainfall between August 27th and August 29th.  Strong southerly flow during the rainfall event caused south-facing slopes of the mountains across Southcentral to get the highest rainfall totals due to enhancement from upslope flow, including the north end of the Susitna Valley, where 2.5 to locally 6 inches of rainfall was recorded between 8/27 and 8/29.  The runoff from the heavy rainfall pushed multiple waterways across the Susitna Valley into moderate flood stage from around 8/29 to 8/31, including sections of the Talkeetna River, Yentna River and Moose Creek.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Yentna River at Lake Creek entered flood stage on the afternoon of August 28th, then rose to a record crest around 22.56 feet in moderate flood stage by August 29th.  River levels remained near the record crest through the morning of August 31st, then began dropping back below flood stage by the evening of August 31st.  Observers along the river between Skwentna and Lake Creek reported that numerous cabins in the area were flooded during this time, with many cabins also left without power due to their generators flooding.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: On August 31st, a resident of Petersville reported that the road along Cache Creek had been totally washed out in several places due to flooding along the creek itself, and the washouts had cut off residents from the main road network for several days.  The resident also mentioned debris including large logs had washed into the road crossings and that the flood waters had overturned a few unoccupied vehicles.  The creek that caused the flood damage was not gauged, so timing of the flood damage was estimated by comparing to timing of the highest water levels observed on the nearby Moose Creek during the same timeframe at the end of August.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: The flood gauge near Talkeetna at the confluence of the Talkeetna River and Susitna River rose into flood stage around 12 PM AKST August 29th, crested just below major flood stage at 14.93 ft around 11 PM AKST August 29th, then receded back to below minor flood stage by 12 PM AKST August 30th.  This was the third highest crest on record for the gauge, and highest water level recorded since 2012. Pictures from Talkeetna by an NWS employee on 8/30 showed overbank flooding at the end of Main Street.  Low lying areas of Talkeetna, particularly the lower west side of town, experienced flood waters from high water on the Susitna. Worst impacts were to the Alaska Dream Cabins that are located at the west end of Main Street / B Street and by the water. The Alaska River Forecast Center found high water marks of 1-2 ft on several buildings. Despite some raising of buildings, Water reached the lowest few inches to foot of many of the buildings. The Talkeetna River Park and campground experienced flooding as well as the low-lying areas between the campground and revetment.

event_description: Press Release - Governor Dunleavy issues Disaster Declaration for 2026 Spring Floods (5/11/2026)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The 2026 spring breakup along the Yukon River was highly dynamic, defined by a combination of thermal ice decay and severe mechanical ice jams. Because of an exceptionally cold winter and a cool spring, the river ice was thicker than normal and had not deteriorated significantly before the main breakup front arrived. Early-season flooding was driven by localized snowmelt and ice jams on independent river systems and upper sections of the Yukon River.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An ice jam on the Koyukuk River near Hughes impounded a significant volume of water. This caused water levels to submerge properties in the lower sections of the community, directly impacting local residences, school property, and the airport. Local residents and members of the Alaska State EOC indicated that the ice set up late Friday night and then released Saturday afternoon. However, a secondary jam set up soon after which was responsible for sending most of the water into the community.  Numerous families were sheltered at the local community hall which is located on higher ground.

event_description: Press Release - Governor Dunleavy issues Disaster Declaration for 2026 Spring Floods (5/11/2026)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The primary breakup front from the Upper Yukon tracked down through the middle section of the Yukon during the middle part of May. While some snowmelt flooding remained over parts of the Upper Yukon, primary dynamics shifted to significant mechanical ice jam releases, notably near the mouth of the Yuki River jam, which caused rapid surges downstream.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An ice jam near the mouth of the Yuki River released a massive surge of water. As this front surged past Galena and Koyukuk, the Galena river gauge recorded a minor flood crest of 124.8 feet on May 15, before slowly receding into action stage (123.7 feet) by May 17.
